description:
We are Team Dhruva, a group of passionate student innovators interested in space technology, scientific exploration, and solving real-world problems through engineering. Our interests span aerospace, orbital mechanics, Earth observation, software development, and data-driven applications.

We are looking for motivated individuals who enjoy taking on challenging problems, experimenting with new technologies, and building something meaningful as a team.
summary:
Terra Trace is an interactive web app that turns NISAR radar data into a clear picture of how Earth's surface changes. We analysed two NISAR S-band passes over India's Cauvery delta, 6 and 18 October 2026, at the start of the northeast monsoon, when cloud hides the region from optical satellites. Our pipeline checks that the two scenes are truly comparable, measures how the HH and HV radar echoes changed, and groups the significant changes into mapped regions with their area in hectares. Each region comes with its evidence, a hypothesis for the cause, and what radar alone cannot prove.

Users explore the results through a guided story, a before/after swipe, an evidence map, and charts that pair the radar with rainfall data. The findings: about 76 mm of rain fell between the passes, paddy fields and the Vedaranyam swamp went dark, which suggests standing water, and the uplands brightened, consistent with wetter soil. Terra Trace also flags false changes, such as radio interference, instead of reporting them. It gives farmers, disaster teams and wetland managers trustworthy answers when the sky is closed.
details:
Terra Trace

Our Github Repository : https://github.com/jeevankumar-m/Terra-Trace

What it does and how it works

Terra Trace turns NISAR radar observations into an interactive map and story that show where Earth's surface changed, how confident we are, and why it might have happened.

  1. Ingest. It reads NISAR S-band L2-GCOV products. These are geocoded, terrain-corrected HH and HV backscatter, stored as HDF5 files of about 11 GB each.
    • same track, frame, orbit direction, bandwidth mode and polarization
    • aligned grids and valid overlap
  2. Align and clean. Both dates are put on one grid with a joint valid-pixel mask. Speckle is reduced by averaging 5×5 pixels, and the open sea is excluded.
  3. Measure change. Backscatter is converted to decibels, and ΔHH, ΔHV and Δ(HH/HV) are computed per pixel. A robust median/MAD z-score marks unusual change, and connected regions are measured in hectares.
    • a pattern label (HH-dominant, HV-dominant, dual-channel or ambiguous)
    • an evidence level with its reasons
    • a plain-language hypothesis for the physical cause
    • what radar alone cannot prove
  4. Add context. Daily rainfall from 12 towns and a Sentinel-2 optical basemap.
    • Story: a guided tour
    • Explore: the change map plus evidence
    • Compare: a before/after swipe with play
    • Insights: charts
    • Method: how it works and the data sources

First study: the Cauvery delta, Tamil Nadu (10,506 km²), using NISAR passes on 6 and 18 October 2026.

  • Rain: about 76 mm fell between the passes.
  • Dark paddies: fields across the eastern delta darkened (likely standing water).
  • Swamp: the Vedaranyam swamp darkened across 1,717 ha.
  • Wetter uplands: the uplands brightened by about 1 dB (wetter soil).
  • Interference caught: a 3,762 ha false signal near Thanjavur was flagged as radio interference.

Benefits

  • Sees through cloud, day or night. It works exactly when optical satellites fail: during the monsoon.
  • No radar expertise needed. It turns complex HDF5 radar products into a story, a map and plain language.
  • Trustworthy. Every number traces to exact scene IDs and processing steps, and artifacts are flagged rather than hidden.
  • Fast and scalable. A whole delta runs in about 80 seconds on a laptop, and new 12-day passes can be added.
  • Free to run. It deploys as a static site with no server costs.
  • Shareable. Results export as GeoJSON, CSV and a one-page evidence report for GIS teams and officials.

Intended impact

  • Agriculture officers: track flooding and samba-season transplanting across rice belts.
  • Disaster-response teams: spot monsoon waterlogging while the sky is still cloudy.
  • Wetland managers: monitor swamps and coastal sanctuaries such as Point Calimere.
  • Students and the public: learn how radar "sees" roughness and moisture.

Long term, NISAR's 12-day repeat cycle can turn Terra Trace into a continuous, transparent monitoring tool.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: Python, TypeScript, HTML/CSS
  • Data processing: h5py, rasterio/GDAL, NumPy, SciPy, Shapely, pyproj
  • Backend (live mode): FastAPI, rio-tiler (map tiles from Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs)
  • Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, MapLibre GL 5
  • Data: NISAR S-band L2-GCOV (ISRO/NRSC Bhoonidhi), Open-Meteo rainfall (ERA5), EOX Sentinel-2 cloudless basemap, OpenStreetMap labels, NASA/JPL imagery
  • Testing and QA: pytest (28 tests), Playwright (visual checks)
  • Deployment: Vercel , GitHub
  • Development aids: Claude Code (AI coding assistant), VS Code
  • Hardware: a standard Windows laptop, with no special hardware or paid cloud computing

How it's creative

  • It tells a story, not just shows a map. Chapters guide anyone from "what is radar?" to what changed and why.
  • It is honest about uncertainty. Every finding pairs a hypothesis with "what radar cannot tell us yet".
  • It catches its own mistakes. The largest "change" turned out to be moving radio interference, and the app shows judges how it caught it.
  • It makes radar colour intuitive. Dual-pol composites and a red/cyan change composite read like a weather map.
  • It adds a time dimension. A swipe-and-play comparison shows the monsoon arriving.
  • It is cheap to share. All results are precomputed, so the whole app is a free static website.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific validity: only truly comparable scenes are compared, speckle and open sea are handled, and the threshold is robust rather than a fixed cut-off.
  • Honesty: no invented data, causes framed as hypotheses, and synthetic test data never shown as real.
  • Data limits: two dates show a difference, not a trend. Tide and wind affect water, and residual interference exists in this product version.
  • Usability: a clean design, plain-language copy, and a 60-second path for judges.
  • Cost and access: free data and tools, free hosting, and it runs on a normal laptop.
  • Time: this was a 48-hour hackathon, so scope was frozen around the core comparison, with clear next steps (more dates, optical corroboration).
  • Licensing and credit: every dataset and image is attributed.
